newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon's big two banks pile on the capital.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon's big two banks pile on the capital.

text.p: Banque du Liban et d'Outre Mer (BLOM) became on Wednesday the second Beirut bank to announce a big year-end capital increase and bankers said the trend would put pressure on a host of smaller banks to increase capital or merge.
BLOM followed Banque de la Mediterranee of billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri in reporting that it had doubled capital at the end of 1996.

It said shareholders' equity had been increased from $77 million to over $150 million. This put it in second place behind Mediterranee whose Chairman Mustafa Razian said on Tuesday it had increased capital from $102 million to $220 million.
Mediterranee ranked as Lebanon's top bank in 1995 by most criteria except for customer deposits in which BLOM was biggest. Both had total assets of around $1.9 billion at end 1995.

BLOM also said in a statement announcing the capital increase that it had acquired all shares in Paris-based Banque Banorabe-France which has branches in London, Dubai, Sharjah and Muscat and wholly owns Geneva-based Banque Banorient-Suisse.
This made BLOM "the Lebanese bank with the largest presence in major European and Arab financial centres," it said.

The capital increases set Mediterranee and BLOM apart as the giants of Lebanon's crowded banking sector, with Banque Audi trailing in third place with $63 million capital. Only six other banks have shareholders' equity of more than $20 million.

The big two have increased capital sharply following Lebanon's 1975-90 civil war. Since 1993 BLOM's capital has jumped from $19 million to $150 million and Mediterranee from $15 million to $212 million. Mediterranee's Razian says his target is $500 million by the year 2,000.

BLOM did not immediately say how it carried out its latest capital increase, but Razian said on Tuesday Mediterranee's came from 1996 profits of about $20 million and in cash from its shareholder, Hariri.

The approach of the big two appeared to differ from other dynamic banks like Audi, Byblos Bank and Banque Libanaise pour le Commerce which in the past 17 months have raised capital through public or private share issues on the local and international markets.

A dealer with another Beirut bank said the BLOM and Mediterranee increases emphasises the gap between Lebanon's bigger banks and the host of smaller, family-owned institutions, many of which had capital of only $2-3 million.
"This means we will now have two tiers of banks. The gap between the strongly capitalised banks and others is getting wider," the dealer said.

"It will put a bit of pressure on small banks to do something about their capital and make them think hard about merging," he said. "They have been talking about mergers for two or three years but now it is becoming more urgent for smaller banks to do something."
According to Bilanbanques 1996, a compilation of data on the Lebanese banking sector, only 17 of the 69 listed banks had more than $10 million shareholders' equity at the end of 1995.
Of the rest, 19 had less than $3 million and the others ranged from $3 million to $9 million.

"The less capitalised banks are going to find it increasingly hard," the dealer said. "Why should anyone put money into banks with $2-$3 million capital if they can put it into the big banks with $200 million capital?"
